questions.stem: FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES were added to the Indian Constitution by the:
questions.explanation: 42nd Amendment ('mini-Constitution', 1976) — added Fundamental Duties as Part IV-A (Article 51A). Originally 10 duties, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th duty — parents to provide education to children aged 6-14.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The CURRENT number of Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution is:
questions.explanation: 11 Fundamental Duties after the 86th Amendment (2002) added the duty of parents to provide education opportunities to children aged 6-14 years. Listed under Article 51A (a) to (k).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY (DPSP) are enshrined in:
questions.explanation: Part IV (Art 36-51) — DPSP. Part III — Fundamental Rights (Art 12-35). Part IV-A — Fundamental Duties (Art 51A). DPSPs are NON-JUSTICIABLE (Art 37) but 'fundamental in the governance of the country'. Inspired by the Irish Constitution.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is a GANDHIAN DPSP?
questions.explanation: Classification: Socialist (Art 38, 39, 41, 42, 43), Gandhian (Art 40, 43, 46, 47, 48), Liberal-Intellectual (Art 44, 45, 48, 49, 50, 51). Village panchayats, promotion of cottage industries, prohibition of intoxicating drinks, cow protection = Gandhian principles.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 51 of the Indian Constitution relates to:

options.option_text: Promotion of international peace and security (DPSP)

questions.explanation: Article 51 — Last DPSP — directs the State to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which country's constitution inspired the concept of DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES?
questions.explanation: Irish Constitution (1937) — DPSP. USA — Fundamental Rights, judicial review. UK — parliamentary form, single citizenship. France — liberty/equality/fraternity in the Preamble. Canada — federal system. Japan — procedure of Supreme Court.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The distinction between DPSP and FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS is that:

options.option_text: DPSP are justiciable; FRs are non-justiciable
FRs are justiciable; DPSP are non-justiciable

questions.explanation: FR (Part III) — enforceable in courts through writs under Art 32/226. DPSP (Part IV) — Art 37 says they are 'not enforceable by any court', but 'fundamental in governance'. Over time, courts have expanded FRs to absorb DPSP values (e.g., Art 21 right to life now includes clean environment, livelihood, education).
